doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

title: Compton Community Center dance, tunes, and time versus perfect notes
summary: The first gig was a dance playing standards and blues with Big Jay McNeely around. Smith argues that good time matters more than correct notes and that he is now a moldy fig wanting swing.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yes. Was that first gig at the Compton Community Center — was that a dance?
And what kind of tunes would they have been playing?
Well we were playing things like “Moonlight in Vermont,” “Blue Moon,” and there was a saxophone player out here, Big Jay McNeely.

And we were playing all that kind of stuff you know. It was basically blues, which I didn’t know was blues, and you just hammer in, you know bang bang bang, just hammer in. And you know the funny thing is if you get two bass players play, and one guy plays perfect notes and doesn’t have great time, and the other guy doesn’t know a damn thing and has good time, that will make the band feel good. But the guy with bad time will mess everything up. So it’s this music. It’s music which is kind of evolved from African rhythm. That’s what it’s totally dependent upon. And that’s one of the things I miss about the most modern music, the jazz music where they don’t have any time going. It’s like, “Come on guys, come on.” You know. But then I realize I’m like — when I was in my twenties or something and the older guys, they’d say, “Well what’s wrong with the melody?” You know. “What’s wrong with playing the melody?” You know. And they were the moldy figs and now I’m a moldy fig you know.
I want it to swing, man, you know?

I used to belong to, I don’t know if it’s the musicians’ union or people who made mutes or something, they used to send, if you purchased enough material they used to send you a bumper sticker that would say, “Play the Melody.”
